problem: Visual navigation systems handle goal-directed navigation and goal-agnostic exploration with separate models. ViNT, for example, pairs a goal-conditioned policy with a 300M-parameter image-diffusion subgoal generator, which adds complexity and compute. Unimodal or regression policies (ViNT, VIB latent models, discretized autoregressive) fail to model the multimodal action distributions that undirected exploration needs, which leads to collisions or averaged actions.
motivation: In unseen environments a robot given a goal image often must first search for the goal, so it needs both task-agnostic exploratory behavior and task-specific goal-reaching. The authors observe that a single high-capacity, expressive policy could represent both. They argue that a Transformer encoder combined with an action diffusion decoder provides the capacity and the multimodal distribution modelling (e.g., both left and right at a junction, but never into a wall) needed to share one policy across the two modes.
key_idea: Train one Transformer-encoded diffusion policy whose goal token can be masked out by attention, so the same network samples multimodal collision-free exploratory action sequences (goal masked) or goal-directed actions (goal unmasked), and plug it into a topological-graph frontier-exploration system.
insight: Modelling actions directly with diffusion, rather than generating subgoal images, gives good multimodal coverage at a fraction of the size. It reaches 98% exploration success with 0.2 collisions using 19M parameters, versus 77% and 1.7 collisions for 335M-parameter Subgoal Diffusion. Qualitatively, the Autoregressive baseline collapses to mostly unimodal (averaged) predictions despite its categorical output. Goal masking costs nothing: the unified policy matches dedicated policies (98% undirected, same as a Diffusion Policy; 92% goal-conditioned, same as the ViNT policy; Table 2), which suggests shared representations and affordances. The encoder and masking mechanism matter a lot (Table 3): the ViNT encoder with attention goal masking gets 98%, versus Early-Fusion CNN with goal dropout 68%, Late-Fusion CNN 52%, and ViT with attention masks 32%, the last attributed to optimization difficulty when training end-to-end with diffusion.
method: ViNT-style encoder: EfficientNet-B0 ψ encodes each of the current and past P RGB frames independently. A goal-fusion EfficientNet φ(o_t, o_g) encodes the observation and goal jointly. Both produce 256-dim tokens, which a 4-layer, 4-head Transformer turns into the context vector c_t.

Attention-based goal masking: a binary mask m blocks attention to the goal token (c_t = f(ψ(o_i), φ(o_t,o_g), m)). In training m ~ Bernoulli(p_m=0.5). At test time m=1 gives undirected exploration and m=0 gives goal-image reaching.

Action diffusion head: a 1D conditional U-Net noise predictor ε_θ (15 conv layers), conditioned on c_t, denoises a Gaussian sample into a future action sequence a_{t:t+H}. It uses a DDPM with a square-cosine noise schedule and K=10 denoising steps, and models only the conditional p(a|c_t) so it runs in real time.

Temporal distance head f_d: predicts the temporal distance between observation and goal from c_t. It is trained with an MSE loss weighted by λ=1e-4 alongside the diffusion noise MSE, end-to-end, and is used to build and localize graph edges.

Topological memory + frontier exploration (ViKiNG setup): the robot builds a graph online, with observation images as nodes and edges set by the predicted distances. A high-level planner drives the robot to unexplored frontiers using samples from the undirected mode, and plans subgoal sequences over the graph for goal navigation.

Training: the GNM + SACSoN datasets (>100 h of real-world multi-robot trajectories). AdamW with lr 1e-4, cosine schedule with warmup, 30 epochs, batch size 256. The whole model is 19M parameters and runs onboard (Jetson Orin).

setting.backbone: EfficientNet-B0 encoders + 4-layer Transformer (ViNT-style) + 1D conditional U-Net diffusion head (trained from scratch, end-to-end)
setting.training_data: GNM + SACSoN datasets: heterogeneous real-world trajectories from multiple ground robots, including pedestrian-rich environments, >100 hours total
setting.observation: monocular RGB (current + past context frames), plus an optional RGB goal image
setting.action_space: predicted future waypoint/action sequence a_{t:t+H} (continuous), sampled via diffusion; executed on a ground robot
setting.privileged: none for exploration; goal-conditioned navigation uses a topological graph built from a prior traversal of the environment (pre-exploration)

numbers_note: All results come from real-world robot experiments; no simulator or standard benchmark is used. Only success rate and mean collisions are reported, and the number of trials is not given. The paper is inconsistent about the environment count ('6 distinct' vs 'Table 1 ... 5 challenging environments'). Table II undirected success (98%) equals the Table I exploration number. Table III ablation variants (Late Fusion CNN 52%/3.2, Early Fusion CNN 68%/1.5, ViT 32%/2.5 on exploration) are not listed as separate entries.
results: In real-world exploration, NoMaD reaches 98% success with 0.2 collisions per experiment. The strongest published baseline, ViNT with Subgoal Diffusion (335M params), gets 77% and 1.7; Autoregressive gets 90%/2.0. NoMaD does this with 15× fewer parameters (19M) and runs onboard. For image-goal navigation in known environments it matches the best baselines at 90%. The unified policy equals dedicated Diffusion Policy (98% undirected) and ViNT (92% goal-conditioned) policies.
limitations: Goals can only be specified as images; language or GPS/coordinate goals are not supported.
High-level exploration is plain frontier-based without semantic priors; the authors note that smarter region selection could help.

Evaluation is small-scale and real-world only: a handful of environments, success and collisions only, trial counts unstated, and no standard simulated benchmark, so comparison with other embodied-nav work is hard.
